heuristics: Before emitting a push intent, ensure the required standing cell (behind the box, opposite the push direction) is reachable by walking in the current state; if not, first plan pushes that open a corridor to that cell or abandon that push direction.
Treat each push as requiring a 2-cell feasibility check: (1) standing cell is walk-reachable now, and (2) destination cell (in push direction) is empty/goal; reject intents failing either check.

Do not assume you can "walk around" a box later: once a box is pushed into a narrow passage, corner-adjacent to walls, or against another box, it may permanently block access to the standing cells needed for future pushes.

Prefer pushes that preserve player access to both sides of boxes in tight areas; avoid moves that reduce a box to having only one accessible pushing side unless that box is already effectively finalized on a goal.

When operating in corridors (1-tile wide paths), recognize that a box becomes direction-locked: you can only push it forward while you can stand behind it; avoid pushing a box deeper if you still need to push it sideways later.
Avoid pushing boxes into non-goal corners (a cell with two perpendicular walls) or into wall-bounded alcoves unless it is a goal cell; this commonly creates immediate or inevitable deadlock.

Avoid creating 2x2 blocks of walls/boxes (or box+wall patterns) that prevent any box movement; treat such local patterns as deadlock unless all involved boxes are on goals and do not need to move again.

Do not push a box flush against a wall if its remaining needed movement would require pulling it away (impossible); only commit to wall-adjacent placements when the goal lies along that wall and the box can be pushed straight to completion.

In multi-box regions, avoid pushing a box to become adjacent (side-by-side) with another box in a narrow space unless you have confirmed future standing-cell access for separating them; paired boxes often block each other’s required push positions.
Maintain at least one “circulation loop” (a walkable cycle) in congested rooms; if your pushes break the loop into a tree-like space, you may lose the ability to reach critical standing cells.
Treat boxes already on goals as potential obstacles: do not use them as temporary parking in chokepoints if that would block access routes needed to maneuver other boxes.
Choose an ordering that solves boxes in the most constrained areas first (deep corners, dead-end corridors, narrow pockets) before pushing boxes that will restrict mobility in the central workspace.

If multiple goals exist in a room, avoid committing a box to a goal that blocks passage to other goals unless you have verified alternate access; a correct placement can still be strategically blocking.

When a planned push would require standing in a cell that is currently enclosed by walls/boxes (a pocket), treat that pocket as unreachable until explicitly opened by moving a blocking box; do not schedule pushes that depend on entering unopened pockets.

To prevent plan exhaustion, generate pushes via a goal-directed macro strategy (e.g., pick a target box, select a candidate path of pushes toward an assigned goal, and verify reachability/deadlock at each step) rather than emitting many unverified local pushes.

In open areas, still apply deadlock screening: a single careless push can freeze a box against boundary walls or create an unsplittable cluster; always run a local deadlock heuristic before accepting a push intent.
